one_liner: Small embeddable R7RS Scheme bytecode VM in C; ran recursive fib(34) about 1.3x faster than PUC Lua in Scriptorium 2015.
what_it_does: Chibi-Scheme is a library-first R7RS-small Scheme meant to be linked into C programs as an extension language, with a sample chibi-scheme REPL on top. You create a context (its own heap, stack and environment) with sexp_make_eval_context, load the standard environment, then call sexp_eval_string, sexp_load or sexp_apply; C primitives are added through its FFI or stub generator. It is a different language and API from Lua, not a drop-in replacement.
how_it_is_fast: Source is macro-expanded and compiled to a compact bytecode run by a switch-dispatched stack VM (vm.c), after a simplify pass that does dead-code elimination, constant folding and propagation of non-mutated let bindings. Top-level references compile to a direct read of the binding cell (SEXP_OP_GLOBAL_KNOWN_REF), fixnums are tagged immediates with inline add/compare opcodes, and memory is managed by a custom precise, non-moving mark-and-sweep GC. Nothing here is unusual for a bytecode VM; the speed edge in the benchmark is small.
when_to_use: You want Scheme (hygienic syntax-rules and low-level macros, call/cc, proper tail calls, R7RS libraries) as the scripting layer of a C or C++ application.
You need several fully isolated interpreters in one process: independent contexts have separate heaps and can run in different OS threads without locking.
Integer- and call-heavy script code where PUC Lua 5.3-era interpreter speed is acceptable and a small, dependency-free interpreter is wanted.
Unix-like targets, iOS, Android or Emscripten/WebAssembly builds where the standard Makefile works.
when_not_to_use: Raw script speed is the priority: on the same Scriptorium page LuaJIT (0.111 s) and even LuaJIT with the JIT off (0.521 s) and Pawn (0.719 s) beat chibi (1.009 s).
Float-heavy numeric code: flonums are heap-allocated doubles by default (immediate flonums are an experimental, single-precision option), so each float result allocates.
Your users expect Lua or JavaScript syntax, or your engine already has Lua bindings (sol2, LuaBridge3).

Native Windows desktop: README-win32.md calls support limited (R7RS-small libraries only; (chibi net), (chibi process), (chibi time) not ported; make install unsupported; degraded flonum precision on MSVC).
Text processing that indexes strings: strings are UTF-8, so string-ref and string-set! are O(n) unless built with SEXP_USE_STRING_INDEX_TABLE.

integration.form: shared lib (libchibi-scheme) or static lib, plus the lib/ tree of Scheme module files needed at runtime for (scheme base); CMake example for Visual Studio
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler with GNU make (Makefile builds with -O3 by default); Visual Studio 2017, MinGW32/64 or MSYS on Windows; minimum C standard not documented
integration.platforms: 32- and 64-bit Linux, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, DragonFlyBSD, macOS, Plan 9, iOS, Android, ARM, Emscripten; limited native Windows
integration.thread_safety: Independent contexts with separate heaps may run concurrently in different OS threads; contexts sharing a heap (children of one parent) must stay on one thread; SRFI 18 green threads run inside a single VM; SRFI-27 is not thread-safe on Windows.

gotchas: Harness asymmetry behind the 1.3x: tests/fib.lua defines fibR as a global, so every recursive call does a hash lookup in the globals table, while chibi compiles its top-level fibr reference to a direct cell read; the idiomatic Lua form (local function) was not measured and would narrow the gap. The table also reports the minimum over separate sessions: bench.csv holds two Lua runs (2.359 s and 1.341 s) and chibi was timed later in its own session (1.010, 1.009, 1.029 s), not interleaved with Lua.

The Lua binary is not pinned: run.bat calls a bare 'lua' from the repo root, which has no lua.exe, so the interpreter on PATH ran (the table links LuaDist/lua); the vendored lua/lua-5.3.1 tree is not proven to be the one timed. Chibi was 0.7.3 then; the current release is 0.12.0.

Precise GC: C code that holds Scheme objects across allocating calls must declare and protect them with sexp_gc_varN / sexp_gc_preserveN / sexp_gc_releaseN, or they can be collected underneath you. Contexts live inside the GC heap and cannot be free()d or held in a C++ smart pointer; use sexp_destroy_context.

Continuations do not capture C frames, so call/cc across a Scheme-to-C-to-Scheme chain (load, eval, your own callbacks) may misbehave; issue #808 (2022, closed) reported segfaults when the sources were compiled as C++, so build them as C and link from C++.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick chibi over NekoVM, TinyVM or Pawn (all near it on the same Scriptorium fib table) when you want a standards-conforming Scheme with macros, continuations and isolated multi-heap embedding; pick Luau or Daslang instead when interpreter throughput matters more than the language.
verified_claims_summary: In r-lyeh's Scriptorium (July 2015, AMD A10 3.8 GHz, Windows 7 64-bit, VS2015 RC or VS2013, flags not stated), whole-process time for recursive fib(34) averaged over 5 runs was 1.009 s for chibi 0.7.3 versus 1.341 s for the PATH 'lua' binary (version unconfirmed), about 1.33x; startup is included and each figure is the best of several logged sessions.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-27, release 0.12.0) and BSD-3-Clause, so copyable; the only speed evidence is one 2015 micro-benchmark with a harness asymmetry that penalises Lua (global function lookup per call) and min-over-sessions reporting, so treat the margin over Lua as roughly parity.
